scenes.headline: Memory Management & GIL
scenes.subtitle: How Python allocates, frees, and locks
scenes.narration: Understanding how Python manages memory and why the Global Interpreter Lock exists is what separates engineers who guess at performance from those who reason about it precisely.

scenes.headline: How Python frees memory
items: Reference counting frees objects instantly when their count hits zero
A cyclic garbage collector reclaims reference cycles counting alone cannot
Small objects are pooled and reused rather than returned to the OS
scenes.narration: Python's primary mechanism is reference counting: every object tracks how many names point to it, and it is freed the instant that count reaches zero. Reference counting cannot handle objects that point at each other in a cycle, so a separate generational garbage collector periodically hunts those cycles down. For efficiency, small integers and short strings are pooled and reused, which is why memory usage does not always shrink after you delete data.

scenes.headline: What the GIL actually does
nodes: It must acquire the GIL first
Only one thread holds it at a time
GIL released on I/O or every few milliseconds
scenes.narration: The Global Interpreter Lock is a single mutex that any thread must hold to execute Python bytecode. Because only one thread can hold it at a time, CPU-bound threads take turns rather than running together. The lock is released during I/O waits and at regular intervals, which is exactly why threading still helps I/O-bound workloads but never CPU-bound ones.

scenes.headline: Escaping the GIL

columns.title: C extensions
points: Heavy work runs in native code

scenes.narration: There are two proven ways around the GIL for heavy computation. Multiprocessing gives each worker its own interpreter and therefore its own lock, unlocking every core at the price of pickling data between processes. Alternatively, native extensions like NumPy and PyArrow release the GIL while they crunch numbers in C, giving you parallelism inside a single process. Choose processes for pure-Python compute, and native libraries when your data already lives in them.

scenes.headline: Inspecting memory with tracemalloc
scenes.code:
import tracemalloc

tracemalloc.start()

rows = [dict(id=i, payload="x" * 1000) for i in range(100000)]

current, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
print(f"current={current/1e6:.1f}MB peak={peak/1e6:.1f}MB")
tracemalloc.stop()
scenes.narration: The tracemalloc module lets you measure allocations rather than guess about them. After calling start, any objects you create are tracked, and get_traced_memory reports both current and peak usage. This is the first tool to reach for when a pipeline mysteriously balloons in memory, because it points you at exactly which allocations are responsible.

scenes.headline: Practical memory tips
items: Use __slots__ on classes with millions of instances to skip per-object dicts
Stream with generators instead of materializing giant lists
Watch for lingering references in caches and closures that block collection
scenes.narration: Defining __slots__ on a heavily instantiated class removes each object's per-instance dictionary, cutting memory dramatically at scale. Streaming data through generators avoids ever holding the whole dataset in RAM. And the most common leak in long-running services is not a leak at all but forgotten references living in caches or closures that quietly prevent collection.

scenes.text: Reference counting frees most objects instantly, the GC handles cycles, and the GIL means threads share one interpreter — use processes or C extensions for real CPU parallelism.
scenes.narration: Keep the mental model clear: reference counting and the cyclic collector manage your memory, while the GIL governs concurrency. When you need true multi-core computation, reach for processes or GIL-releasing native libraries.
